Weak-Instrument Inference and Model Diagnostics in Double Machine Learning for Linear Instrumental Variable Models

Airui Meng ††thanks: Teachers College, Columbia University, 525 West 120th Street, New York, NY 10027, USA. Email: am6817@tc.columbia.edu.
October 2026
Abstract

We study weak-instrument-robust inference in partially linear instrumental-variables models with learned nuisances. Building on an i.i.d. uniform-size baseline, we establish uniform asymptotic validity of clustered cross-fitted Anderson–Rubin inference and cross-fitted score inference under the stated sampling and nuisance-rate conditions. Extensions establish Anderson–Rubin validity for survey-weighted target laws and fold-nested generated instruments. A supporting population benchmark shows that prediction-optimal instrument residualization maximizes concentration when the treatment nuisance is correctly specified. A five-design diagnostic portfolio, a known-truth Monte Carlo, and an exploratory selector examine how nuisance specification and estimation affect realized strength and inference.

Keywords: Double machine learning, Partially linear model, Weak instruments, Identification-robust inference, Model selection.

JEL classification: C14, C21, C26, C55.

1 Introduction

Double machine learning (DML) enables estimation and inference in partially linear instrumental-variables (PLIV) models with flexible, high-dimensional controls. Under strong identification and suitable regularity and nuisance-estimation rate conditions, cross-fitted orthogonal scores deliver asymptotically normal estimators and valid conventional inference (Chernozhukov et al., 2018). When residualized identification is weak, these guarantees need not apply. The central problem is to obtain valid confidence sets after nuisance estimation and selection without requiring a strong residualized first stage.

Applied sampling designs introduce additional requirements. With clustered observations, score variation and nuisance-estimation errors must be controlled at the cluster level. Survey weights can change the target law and the conditional means used for residualization. A generated instrument adds construction error and must be estimated without using its inference fold. Validity for independent observations and an observed instrument under an unweighted target law does not by itself establish validity in these settings.

Learner sensitivity motivates a related diagnostic question. In CollegeDistance, Çetin (2026a) finds that regularized linear learners produce estimates close to conventional two-stage least squares, whereas random forests produce near-zero estimates with small Wald standard errors. Çetin (2026a) introduces residualized concentration under strong identification and proposes absorption of identifying variation as an explanation. Two questions guide our analysis: how to conduct inference when residualized identification is weak, and how to interpret strength differences across nuisance learners.

We address these questions in two steps. The main inferential results establish uniform asymptotic validity of clustered cross-fitted Anderson–Rubin inference and cross-fitted score inference under the stated conditions. AR extensions cover survey-weighted target laws and fold-nested generated instruments. A supporting population benchmark holds the instrument and conditioning set fixed and takes the treatment nuisance at its true conditional mean. In that setting, prediction-optimal instrument residualization maximizes concentration, providing a reference for interpreting realized learner differences.

For inference, we use the Anderson–Rubin test (Anderson and Rubin, 1949) and related identification-robust procedures (Kleibergen, 2005; Moreira, 2003), which control size under weak identification. We also assess realized first-stage strength using a robust Wald statistic, which coincides with the Montiel Olea and Pflueger (2013) effective FF in the single-instrument case.11 1 See also Lee et al. (2022) and Andrews et al. (2019). Applying these tests to cross-fitted PLIV moments requires control of errors from nuisance fitting and selection, together with a consistent covariance estimator under the relevant sampling design. These requirements underlie the validity results below; the effective-FF statistic serves as a diagnostic of realized strength.

We make three contributions, centered on the validity of identification-robust inference after nuisance learning.

  • •

    Weak-instrument-robust inference for applied PLIV designs. We derive the local-to-zero limit of the just-identified cross-fitted estimator and its feasible Wald statistic, clarifying why a small standard error does not establish reliable precision under weak identification (Proposition 2). Within the leakage-free nested cross-fitting framework of Çetin (2026b), we establish uniform asymptotic validity of the clustered Anderson–Rubin procedure and the cross-fitted score statistic under the stated sampling and nuisance-rate conditions (Theorems 1 and 2). We further develop extensions for survey-weighted target laws and fold-nested generated instruments (Propositions –). The generated-instrument extension covers AR inference; its score counterpart is established in the single-instrument case. Monte Carlo experiments evaluate finite-sample coverage and the informativeness of the resulting confidence sets, including stress settings with coverage shortfalls.

  • •

    Population optimality of instrument residualization. We establish a population benchmark for interpreting sensitivity to nuisance learners. Holding the instrument and conditioning set fixed, and taking the treatment nuisance at its true conditional mean, the prediction-optimal instrument residualization maximizes residualized concentration over all admissible residualizations (Proposition 3). Recovering the instrument’s conditional mean therefore entails no population concentration loss. Together with estimand invariance under the maintained homogeneous-coefficient PLIV model (Proposition 1), this result distinguishes changes in identification strength from changes in the parameter being estimated and provides a benchmark against which observed learner differences can be assessed.

  • •

    Empirical diagnosis of learner sensitivity. Across four of the five applications, we combine nuisance-fit diagnostics, residualized first-stage strength, and identification-robust confidence sets to investigate why estimates and inference vary across learners. The evidence supports distinct diagnoses: overfit dilution in the examiner design, geographic fold leakage and coupled nuisance misspecification in CollegeDistance, and reduced conditional relevance along a fixed-sample, fixed-instrument Card control ladder. A randomized application provides a stable-strength benchmark. Known-truth simulations isolate the role of treatment-nuisance specification: the relative strength ranking of flexible and regularized linear residualizations reverses between correctly specified and misspecified treatment nuisances. These comparisons show how apparently similar empirical patterns can call for different changes to nuisance estimation, cross-fitting, or the interpretation of the conditional design.

Together, these results show why learner choice, residualized instrument strength, and inference must be considered jointly in DML-IV applications.

1.1 Related literature

The analysis builds on Çetin (2026a); Çetin (2026b). Çetin (2026a) introduces residualized concentration and documents learner sensitivity under strong identification; Çetin (2026b) provides leakage-free nested cross-fitting (LF-NCF), identification-aware cross-validation (IACV), and i.i.d. uniform-size AR theory.22 2 The nested selection idea, product-rate architecture, concentration measure, CollegeDistance sensitivity and proposed mechanism, restricted-π\pi analysis, and Angrist–Krueger stress exercise originate in Çetin (2026a). Çetin (2026b) also supplies the tuning-overfit discussion and the ridge-AR and conditional-QLR results drawn on here. Our inferential contribution concerns the additional validity arguments needed for cluster dependence, survey-weighted target laws, and fold-nested instrument construction.33 3 The i.i.d. AR result of Çetin (2026b, Theorem 3) is restated as Theorem  in Supplementary . Çetin (2026c) studies power when a scalar AR direction is learned from a growing instrument dictionary. Here the PLIV moment is fixed and its nuisance functions are selected; our theory establishes size and coverage for that moment under the sampling designs considered.

Ma (2026) is the closest published study. It develops an orthogonalized Anderson–Rubin test for the LATE with high-dimensional covariates and extends the analysis to scores that are linear in the parameter, including the PLIV score, through a cross-fitted conditional QLR test (Appendix B, Example 1). The two approaches share a cross-fitted, Neyman-orthogonal construction and an emphasis on uniform asymptotic validity. Ma’s results are established for i.i.d. observations, an observed instrument, an unweighted target law, and cross-fitted nuisance learners satisfying its regularity and rate conditions. These conditions allow flexible learners; the study does not separately develop selection guarantees for a learner library. Our analysis uses the nested selection framework described above and establishes validity for cluster dependence, survey-weighted target laws, and fold-nested instrument construction. These settings require, respectively, control of cluster-sum remainders, orthogonality under the weighted law, and bounds on instrument-construction error.

An early antecedent of selection-aware IV inference is Belloni et al. (2012), who use lasso to select optimal instruments from a high-dimensional dictionary and provide a sup-score test that is robust to weak identification. The distinction lies in the object of selection: their procedure selects instruments, whereas our analysis concerns the nuisance learners used to residualize the outcome, treatment, and instruments. 44 4 The sup-score procedure of Belloni et al. (2012) uses raw instruments after low-dimensional linear partialling, provides pointwise size control, and does not cross-fit the three PLIV nuisance functions.

A complementary literature develops inference that is robust to the number of instruments. Building on Chao and Swanson (2005) and Hansen et al. (2008), Mikusheva and Sun (2022) construct a jackknife Anderson–Rubin test when the instrument count grows proportionally with sample size. Navjeevan (2026) develops a dimension-agnostic jackknife score statistic, and Lim et al. (2024) propose a dimension-agnostic bootstrap Anderson–Rubin procedure. These studies treat the instruments as fixed, remove controls by exact linear projection, and assume independent observations. Navjeevan (2026, p. 3, fn. 3) identifies accommodating high-dimensional controls while incorporating first-stage information as an open issue. Zhang et al. (2026) combine cross-fitted orthogonal moments and multi-task learning and propose a continuous updating estimator and corresponding Wald statistics that are robust to increasing IV dimensions and high-dimensional covariates. Our orthogonalized, cross-fitted PLIV construction addresses this issue in a complementary setting: the instrument dimension is fixed and moderate, while machine learners accommodate high-dimensional or nonparametric control functions. 55 5 The “cross-fit” variance estimators of Mikusheva and Sun (2022) are leave-one-out variance proxies within a full-sample projection statistic. They differ from the fold-based sample splitting used here to accommodate machine learning. Supplementary discusses their pre-test interpretation of the quarter-of-birth design.

For clustered data, Wang and Zhang (2024) establish the validity of wild bootstrap Anderson–Rubin inference in linear IV models with few large clusters. Their asymptotic framework complements the regime of many moderate clusters in Theorem 1.

Recent panel working papers examine related questions in longitudinal settings. Baiardi et al. (2026) use first differences and apply a panel analogue of the first-stage FF statistic and an Anderson–Rubin test to shift-share migration designs. Avila Márquez (2026) shows that linear reduced-form specifications can make panel instruments spuriously weak and proposes a Super Learner control-function estimator with a generalized concentration parameter. 66 6 Both studies remain unpublished working papers as of this writing.

The examiner-design literature provides another setting in which instrument construction and nuisance learning interact. These designs use the leniency of a quasi-randomly assigned decision-maker as an instrument for treatment (Dobbie et al., 2018; Chyn et al., 2025). Our high-dimensional application uses a fold-nested cluster-jackknife leniency instrument and examines how flexible residualization affects its realized strength.

Finally, a parallel literature on flexible IV methods studies different target parameters. Athey et al. (2019) and Hartford et al. (2017) target heterogeneous effects or structural functions, while Blandhol et al. (2026) study the implicit weighting of the linear IV estimand under flexible controls. These objects differ from the scalar homogeneous-coefficient PLIV parameter maintained here. A like-for-like comparison would therefore first require testing the homogeneity restriction.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the PLIV model and identification results, and Section 3 develops estimation and inference. Section 4 evaluates coverage and nuisance specification in Monte Carlo studies. Section 5 presents the applications through a common diagnostic protocol, comparative evidence, and a cross-application synthesis. Section 6 discusses the implications and limitations and concludes. The Supplementary Material contains proofs, full result tables, and simulation designs (Supplementary –), together with application, selection, and cross-fitting details (Supplementary –).

2 Model and Identification

2.1 Setup

We study the partially linear instrumental-variables (PLIV) model

Y=τ0D+g0(W)+ζ,𝔼[ζ∣Z,W]=0,Y=\tau_{0}\,D+g_{0}(W)+\zeta,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\zeta\mid Z,W]=0,

where DD is a scalar endogenous regressor, ZZ is an instrument of dimension dzd_{z}, WW is a vector of controls, and τ0\tau_{0} is the scalar structural parameter of interest. Estimation rests on the residualized, Neyman-orthogonal PLIV score

ψ⁡(τ,η)=(Z−π⁡(W))​[(Y−μ⁡(W))−τ⁡(D−r⁡(W))],\psi(\tau,\eta)=\big(Z-\pi(W)\big)\big[\,(Y-\mu(W))-\tau\,(D-r(W))\,\big],

where η=(μ,r,π)\eta=(\mu,r,\pi) collects the nuisances, whose true values (subscript 00) are η0=(μ0,r0,π0)\eta_{0}=(\mu_{0},r_{0},\pi_{0}) with μ0​(W)=𝔼​[Y∣W]\mu_{0}(W)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid W], r0​(W)=𝔼​[D∣W]r_{0}(W)=\mathbb{E}[D\mid W], and π0​(W)=𝔼​[Z∣W]\pi_{0}(W)=\mathbb{E}[Z\mid W]. We write residualized variables as Y~=Y−μ0​(W)\tilde{Y}=Y-\mu_{0}(W), D~=D−r0​(W)\tilde{D}=D-r_{0}(W), and Z~=Z−π0​(W)\tilde{Z}=Z-\pi_{0}(W). A naming caution: the classical “first stage” regresses the treatment on the instruments, and π0\pi_{0} is not that object. We call π0\pi_{0} the instrument-residualization nuisance (the residualization, for short). The classical first stage appears here only in residualized form, as the D~\tilde{D}-on-Z~\tilde{Z} relation whose strength §2.3 and §5.1 measure.

We take as given the leakage-safe nested cross-fitting of Çetin (2026a); Çetin (2026b). Nesting matters because, under weak identification, selection that reuses inference observations can distort the null law of identification-robust statistics at first order. The protocol splits the complement of each held-out (inference) fold into an estimation and a selection subsample. Candidate learners for (μ,r,π)(\mu,r,\pi) are fit on the estimation subsample, selected on the selection subsample, and the selected fits evaluate the held-out fold, with no refit on the union. Every selected object is therefore measurable with respect to data disjoint from the fold it scores. Under a product-rate condition and strong identification, Çetin (2026a, Theorem 2) delivers n\sqrt{n}-asymptotic normality of the residualized-IV estimator. Our contribution begins where the strong-identification assumption is relaxed. Before examining inference under weak identification, we first clarify whether the choice of instrument residualization changes the population estimand.

2.2 Estimand invariance across instrument residualizations

Different instrument-residualization learners can produce different estimates, but this does not by itself establish that they target different population parameters. To interpret this sensitivity, we first clarify the role of π\pi in the population PLIV moment. With the outcome and treatment nuisances at their true conditional means, the maintained exogeneity condition ensures that any admissible instrument residualization leaves the moment valid at τ0\tau_{0}. The following proposition establishes the corresponding estimand invariance and consistency result.

Proposition 1 (Estimand invariance and the role of the instrument residualization).

Work at a fixed population under the sampling and moment conditions in Supplementary . Suppose the PLIV model holds with 𝔼[ζ∣Z,W]=0\mathbb{E}[\zeta\mid Z,W]=0 and g:=𝔼⁡[Z~​D~]≠0g:=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Z}\tilde{D}]\neq 0. For any square-integrable, WW-measurable residualization limit π∗\pi_{\ast}, assume Ω∗:=𝔼⁡[(Z−π∗​(W))​(Z−π∗​(W))′]≻0\Omega_{\ast}:=\mathbb{E}[(Z-\pi_{\ast}(W))(Z-\pi_{\ast}(W))^{\prime}]\succ 0. If the cross-fitted fits (μ^,r^,π^)(\hat{\mu},\hat{r},\hat{\pi}) converge to (μ0,r0,π∗)(\mu_{0},r_{0},\pi_{\ast}) in the held-out empirical L2L^{2} norm defined there, the residualized-IV estimator is consistent for τ0\tau_{0}. The limit π∗\pi_{\ast} need not equal π0\pi_{0}. Under these conditions, the choice of instrument residualization can affect residualized concentration without changing the estimand or consistency.

One implication is that a linear instrument residualization can yield a consistent estimator even when π0\pi_{0} is nonlinear: the linear projection remains an admissible limit π∗\pi_{\ast}. Thus, under the stated conditions, changing the instrument-residualization learner does not change the probability limit of the estimator. Differences between finite-sample estimates may nevertheless reflect estimation error or differences in residualized strength. If the outcome or treatment nuisance is misspecified, the conditions supporting this invariance no longer hold. A near-zero estimate under flexible learning therefore does not, by itself, establish either a zero structural effect or a loss of identification.

These conclusions concern the maintained homogeneous-coefficient PLIV model. Under effect heterogeneity, the estimated coefficient may instead represent a weighted average of heterogeneous responses, whose causal interpretation requires separate justification. The target map in Section 5.1 records the statistical and causal targets maintained in each application.

Proposition 1 concerns consistency at a fixed population with nonzero residualized relevance. Supplementary provides the proof and states the scope of the associated precision comparisons. We next examine how weak residualized identification affects the estimator’s sampling distribution and the validity of conventional Wald inference.

2.3 Wald inference under weak residualized identification

Define the per-observation residualized concentration

C=gZ​D′​Ω−1​gZ​D,gZ​D=𝔼⁡[Z~​D~],Ω=𝔼⁡[Z~​Z~′],C=g_{ZD}^{\prime}\,\Omega^{-1}g_{ZD},\qquad g_{ZD}=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Z}\tilde{D}],\quad\Omega=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Z}\tilde{Z}^{\prime}],

and the concentration parameter μ2=n​C\mu^{2}=nC. The classical concentration parameter divides n​CnC by the first-stage error variance and is dimensionless; our μ2\mu^{2} keeps the treatment scale and enters only order and ranking statements within one design. The asymptotic variance of the residualized-IV estimator scales as Var⁡(τ^)∝1/(n​C)=1/μ2\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\tau})\propto 1/(nC)=1/\mu^{2} under conditional homoskedasticity of the score; under bounded conditional heteroskedasticity CC ranks weak-identification strength up to constants (Supplementary ), so a reduction in CC is a loss of identification strength at fixed nn.

The inverse-concentration variance approximation relies on strong identification. When residualized relevance is weak, the validity of the usual normal approximation requires separate examination. In particular, a near-zero estimate with a small reported Wald standard error need not establish a precisely estimated zero. Proposition 2 formalizes this distinction in the just-identified case. It first establishes that rescaling the residualized instrument leaves the Wald variance unchanged, and then characterizes the estimator and feasible Wald statistic under a local-to-zero sequence. The key issue is whether the statistic has the reference distribution required for conventional Wald inference.

Proposition 2 (Scale invariance and Wald inference under weak identification).

In the just-identified case dz=1d_{z}=1, write u=Y~−τ0​D~u=\tilde{Y}-\tau_{0}\tilde{D} for the structural score residual, Σ=𝔼⁡[Z~2​u2]\Sigma=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Z}^{2}u^{2}], and V=Σ/gZ​D2V=\Sigma/g_{ZD}^{2} for the Wald variance. (i) This VV is invariant to the scale of Z~\tilde{Z}: the magnitude of the reported standard error therefore carries no evidence about instrument strength on its own, in either direction. (ii) Under the local-to-zero sequence of Staiger and Stock (1997), gZ​D,n=γ/ng_{ZD,n}=\gamma/\sqrt{n}, the cross-fitted joint limit of Lemma  (Supplementary ) yields: τ^\hat{\tau} is inconsistent and Op​(1)O_{p}(1); the standard error neither vanishes nor explodes (se^\widehat{\mathrm{se}} and se^−1\widehat{\mathrm{se}}^{-1} are both Op​(1)O_{p}(1)); and the statistic whose variance is evaluated at the hypothesized value is asymptotically pivotal in absolute value, its square being exactly the cross-fitted AR statistic of §3. (iii) The feasible Wald statistic (τ^−τ0)/se^​(τ^)(\hat{\tau}-\tau_{0})/\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat{\tau}), whose variance evaluates residuals at τ^\hat{\tau}, is non-pivotal along the sequence for every value of the score correlation ρ=Corr⁡(Z~​u,Z~​D~)\rho=\mathrm{Corr}(\tilde{Z}u,\tilde{Z}\tilde{D}), including ρ=0\rho=0, and is standard normal only in the strong-identification limit. Standard-normal critical values are therefore not generically valid along the sequence, no fixed critical value controls size uniformly over strength and score-correlation configurations, and the nominal 1−α1-\alpha Wald interval does not attain 1−α1-\alpha coverage in general (Supplementary ).

Proposition 2 shows why a near-zero estimate with a small reported Wald standard error need not establish a precisely estimated zero. Along the local-to-zero sequence, the feasible Wald statistic has a nonstandard limiting distribution, so conventional Wald confidence intervals need not attain nominal coverage. This motivates the identification-robust inference procedures described in Section 3.

2.4 The anatomy of concentration loss

Proposition 2 characterizes the consequences of weak residualized identification for conventional Wald inference. We now examine whether the choice of instrument residualization can itself reduce population concentration. Holding the conditioning set fixed and taking the treatment nuisance to be correctly specified, we compare C⁡(π)C(\pi) across admissible residualizations. The following proposition establishes that the true conditional mean π0​(W)=𝔼​[Z∣W]\pi_{0}(W)=\mathbb{E}[Z\mid W] maximizes this population concentration index.

Proposition 3 (Concentration is maximized at the true π0\pi_{0}).

Assume 𝔼​∥Z∥2+𝔼⁡[D2]<∞\mathbb{E}\lVert Z\rVert^{2}+\mathbb{E}[D^{2}]<\infty, that Ω⁡(π0)\Omega(\pi_{0}) is positive definite, and that the relevance vector g=𝔼⁡[Z~0​D~]g=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Z}_{0}\tilde{D}] is nonzero. With the treatment nuisance correctly specified, r=r0=𝔼⁡[D∣W]r=r_{0}=\mathbb{E}[D\mid W], the residualized concentration C⁡(π)=gZ​D​(π)′​Ω​(π)−1​gZ​D​(π)C(\pi)=g_{ZD}(\pi)^{\prime}\,\Omega(\pi)^{-1}g_{ZD}(\pi) satisfies C⁡(π)≤C⁡(π0)C(\pi)\leq C(\pi_{0}) for every square-integrable WW-measurable π\pi, with equality iff π=π0\pi=\pi_{0} when dz=1d_{z}=1, and for dz>1d_{z}>1 iff the perturbation π0−π\pi_{0}-\pi is concentration-neutral (M​Ω​(π0)−1​gZ​D=0M\,\Omega(\pi_{0})^{-1}g_{ZD}=0, with M=𝔼⁡[(π0−π)​(π0−π)′]M=\mathbb{E}[(\pi_{0}-\pi)(\pi_{0}-\pi)^{\prime}]; Supplementary ). The prediction-optimal residualization π0\pi_{0} is therefore concentration-optimal in population: a consistent flexible learner that recovers a nonlinear π0\pi_{0} attains the maximum concentration and cannot lower it.

The proof (Supplementary ) closes only the population channel: realized, finite-sample concentration can still fall, through two diagnosable routes separated by the out-of-fold predictive R2R^{2} of π^\hat{\pi} on ZZ (Roof2​(π^,Z)R^{2}_{\text{oof}}(\hat{\pi};Z)) and the residualized-variance ratio Var⁡(Z~)/Var⁡(Z)\mathrm{Var}(\tilde{Z})/\mathrm{Var}(Z), which are shown as follows.

Under stratified randomization of ZZ given WW the assignment shares are known within strata, so π0\pi_{0} equals those shares; a learner can at most recover them, residualization removes only the across-strata variance of ZZ, and CC is preserved in population up to that design variation. 3 Estimation and Inference

We estimate the PLIV parameter using cross-fitted residualized moments and use Anderson–Rubin (AR) confidence sets as the primary basis for inference under potentially weak residualized identification. Conventional Wald intervals provide a benchmark, while score-based confidence sets provide a complementary procedure with multiple instruments. We first describe estimation and the validity results for AR and score inference under the stated conditions. We then discuss survey weights and generated instruments. Section 5.1 sets out the common diagnostic and reporting protocol for the applications.

3.1 Cross-fitted estimation

We implement the three-way protocol of Section 2.1, with k⁡(i)k(i) denoting observation ii’s outer inference fold. Within each outer training sample, candidate nuisance functions are fitted and tuned on an estimation subsample, then selected on a separate selection subsample using separate prediction criteria for the outcome, treatment, and instrument nuisances. The selected fits are evaluated on the inference fold without refitting on the union of the estimation and selection subsamples. A prespecified learner that undergoes no selection may instead be fitted on the full outer training sample. All fitted objects used for an observation are constructed without using observations in its inference fold.

For clustered data, entire clusters are assigned to folds, and all subsequent estimation and selection splits also partition clusters. The assignment rule uses cluster sizes and, if needed, randomization independent of the observed outcomes, treatments, instruments, and controls. These rules preserve the separation required by the clustered results below.

Write η^−k=(μ^−k,r^−k,π^−k)\hat{\eta}_{-k}=(\hat{\mu}_{-k},\hat{r}_{-k},\hat{\pi}_{-k}) for the nuisance estimates used to evaluate inference fold kk. The estimated residuals are

Y~^i=Yi−μ^−k⁡(i)​(Wi),D~^i=Di−r^−k⁡(i)​(Wi),Z~^i=Zi−π^−k⁡(i)​(Wi).\hat{\tilde{Y}}_{i}=Y_{i}-\hat{\mu}_{-k(i)}(W_{i}),\qquad\hat{\tilde{D}}_{i}=D_{i}-\hat{r}_{-k(i)}(W_{i}),\qquad\hat{\tilde{Z}}_{i}=Z_{i}-\hat{\pi}_{-k(i)}(W_{i}).

Define the pooled moments

g^Z​D=1n​∑iZ~^i​D~^i,g^Z​Y=1n​∑iZ~^i​Y~^i,Ω^=1n​∑iZ~^i​Z~^i′.\hat{g}_{ZD}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\hat{\tilde{Z}}_{i}\hat{\tilde{D}}_{i},\qquad\hat{g}_{ZY}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\hat{\tilde{Z}}_{i}\hat{\tilde{Y}}_{i},\qquad\hat{\Omega}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\hat{\tilde{Z}}_{i}\hat{\tilde{Z}}_{i}^{\prime}.

The residualized-IV estimator is

τ^=g^Z​D′​Ω^−1​g^Z​Yg^Z​D′​Ω^−1​g^Z​D.\hat{\tau}=\frac{\hat{g}_{ZD}^{\prime}\hat{\Omega}^{-1}\hat{g}_{ZY}}{\hat{g}_{ZD}^{\prime}\hat{\Omega}^{-1}\hat{g}_{ZD}}. (1)

For dz=1d_{z}=1, this reduces to the ratio of the residualized instrument–outcome and instrument–treatment moments; for dz>1d_{z}>1, it is the Ω^−1\hat{\Omega}^{-1}-weighted GMM estimator. We report its heteroskedasticity- or cluster-robust sandwich standard error as a conventional benchmark. When strong identification cannot be maintained, Proposition 2 motivates testing the null moment directly and inverting these tests to construct confidence sets.

3.2 Identification-robust inference

3.2.1 Anderson–Rubin statistics

For a candidate value tt, evaluate the cross-fitted null score

ψ^i​(t)=Z~^i​(Y~^i−t​D~^i).\hat{\psi}_{i}(t)=\hat{\tilde{Z}}_{i}\bigl(\hat{\tilde{Y}}_{i}-t\hat{\tilde{D}}_{i}\bigr).

The covariance estimator is recomputed at each tested value. With independent observations, the heteroskedasticity-robust AR statistic is

ARn​(t)=(∑iψ^i​(t))′​(∑iψ^i​(t)​ψ^i​(t)′)−1​(∑iψ^i​(t)).\mathrm{AR}_{n}(t)=\left(\sum_{i}\hat{\psi}_{i}(t)\right)^{\prime}\left(\sum_{i}\hat{\psi}_{i}(t)\hat{\psi}_{i}(t)^{\prime}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i}\hat{\psi}_{i}(t)\right). (2)

Unlike a Wald statistic, this construction evaluates the residual at the hypothesized value and does not divide by an estimated first-stage coefficient. Theorem  of Supplementary , restated from Çetin (2026b, Theorem 3), establishes uniformly correct asymptotic size using χdz2\chi^{2}_{d_{z}} critical values under Assumptions A1–A7. We extend this result to clustered data.

For GG i.i.d. clusters, define

S^c​(t)=∑i∈cψ^i​(t).\hat{S}_{c}(t)=\sum_{i\in c}\hat{\psi}_{i}(t).

The cluster-robust analogue is

ARG​(t)=(∑c=1GS^c​(t))′​(∑c=1GS^c​(t)​S^c​(t)′)−1​(∑c=1GS^c​(t)).\mathrm{AR}_{G}(t)=\left(\sum_{c=1}^{G}\hat{S}_{c}(t)\right)^{\prime}\left(\sum_{c=1}^{G}\hat{S}_{c}(t)\hat{S}_{c}(t)^{\prime}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{c=1}^{G}\hat{S}_{c}(t)\right). (3)

The statistic aggregates scores within clusters before taking outer products. Its validity also requires a cluster-level argument: observation-level splitting need not separate training data from dependent inference observations, and the nuisance-estimation remainders must be controlled for cluster sums.

At the true value, the population score is mean zero regardless of instrument strength. Orthogonality and the nuisance-rate conditions control the effect of estimating the residuals, while cluster aggregation accounts for within-cluster dependence. The proof establishes equivalence to the oracle cluster scores, a cluster-level central limit theorem, and covariance consistency. Conditions C1–C8 in Supplementary require i.i.d. clusters with bounded or suitably controlled random sizes, score moment bounds and a uniformly nonsingular covariance, cluster-level sample splitting, and uniform nuisance and product-rate conditions. Within-cluster dependence is unrestricted subject to these bounds.

Condition C8 also requires exogeneity and stability of nuisance conditional means given cluster size, together with conditional moment and domination bounds. They ensure that the required centering and error bounds remain valid when fold assignment depends on cluster size. These conditions impose no positive lower bound on residualized relevance. The following theorem establishes uniform asymptotic validity under these conditions.

Theorem 1 (Uniform validity of clustered cross-fitted AR inference).

Suppose Conditions C1–C8 in Supplementary hold, with G→∞G\to\infty and fixed dzd_{z}. For any fixed α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1),

supP∈𝒫G|P{ARG(τ0)>χdz,1−α2}−α|⟶0.\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{G}}\left|P\!\left\{\mathrm{AR}_{G}(\tau_{0})>\chi^{2}_{d_{z},1-\alpha}\right\}-\alpha\right|\longrightarrow 0.

Consequently, the inverted set

𝒞AR,G​(1−α)={t∈ℝ:ARG​(t)≤χdz,1−α2}\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{AR},G}(1-\alpha)=\left\{t\in\mathbb{R}:\mathrm{AR}_{G}(t)\leq\chi^{2}_{d_{z},1-\alpha}\right\}

has coverage tending to 1−α1-\alpha uniformly over 𝒫G\mathcal{P}_{G}.

The class 𝒫G\mathcal{P}_{G} includes strong-identification laws and relevance sequences of order G−1/2G^{-1/2}. The same critical values therefore apply across these identification regimes, subject to the stated conditions. The proof is in Supplementary .

3.2.2 Score inference with multiple instruments

The AR statistic evaluates the full dzd_{z}-dimensional vector of null moments. A complementary score statistic projects these moments onto an adjusted Jacobian direction. The two procedures coincide with a single instrument, so the score test provides a distinct inferential option in over-identified models. Because τ\tau is scalar, the score test has a one-degree-of-freedom reference under the conditions stated below.

Define the observation-level Jacobian contribution

q^i=∂tψ^i​(t)=−Z~^i​D~^i.\hat{q}_{i}=\partial_{t}\hat{\psi}_{i}(t)=-\hat{\tilde{Z}}_{i}\hat{\tilde{D}}_{i}.

To cover both sampling schemes, let NN be the number of independent sampling units. For i.i.d. observations, N=nN=n, S^a​(t)=ψ^a​(t)\hat{S}_{a}(t)=\hat{\psi}_{a}(t), and Q^a=q^a\hat{Q}_{a}=\hat{q}_{a}. For clustered observations, N=GN=G, S^a​(t)\hat{S}_{a}(t) is the cluster sum defined above, and Q^a=∑i∈aq^i\hat{Q}_{a}=\sum_{i\in a}\hat{q}_{i}. Set

m^N​(t)\displaystyle\hat{m}_{N}(t) =1N​∑a=1NS^a​(t),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{a=1}^{N}\hat{S}_{a}(t), g^N\displaystyle\hat{g}_{N} =1N​∑a=1NQ^a,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{a=1}^{N}\hat{Q}_{a},
V^f​f​(t)\displaystyle\hat{V}_{ff}(t) =1N​∑a=1NS^a​(t)​S^a​(t)′,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{a=1}^{N}\hat{S}_{a}(t)\hat{S}_{a}(t)^{\prime}, V^θ​f​(t)\displaystyle\hat{V}_{\theta f}(t) =1N​∑a=1N(Q^a−g^N)​S^a​(t)′.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{a=1}^{N}(\hat{Q}_{a}-\hat{g}_{N})\hat{S}_{a}(t)^{\prime}.

The adjusted Jacobian and the cross-fitted score statistic are

D^N​(t)\displaystyle\hat{D}_{N}(t) =g^N−V^θ​f​(t)​V^f​f​(t)−1​m^N​(t),\displaystyle=\hat{g}_{N}-\hat{V}_{\theta f}(t)\hat{V}_{ff}(t)^{-1}\hat{m}_{N}(t), (4)
KN​(t)\displaystyle\mathrm{K}_{N}(t) =N​[m^N​(t)′​V^f​f​(t)−1​D^N​(t)]2D^N​(t)′​V^f​f​(t)−1​D^N​(t).\displaystyle=\frac{N\bigl[\hat{m}_{N}(t)^{\prime}\hat{V}_{ff}(t)^{-1}\hat{D}_{N}(t)\bigr]^{2}}{\hat{D}_{N}(t)^{\prime}\hat{V}_{ff}(t)^{-1}\hat{D}_{N}(t)}. (5)

This is the scalar-parameter score construction of Kleibergen (2005), applied to the cross-fitted moments.

AR validity alone does not establish the joint approximation required by the score statistic. We therefore impose two additional conditions in Supplementary . K1 imposes moment bounds on the stacked score and Jacobian, conditional second-moment bounds, and non-degeneracy of the Jacobian covariance after projection on the score. K3 requires both covariance blocks to use the same sampling-unit aggregation: with clustered data, both the score and the Jacobian are summed within clusters before the covariance blocks are formed. These conditions make the adjusted direction well defined asymptotically even when population relevance approaches zero.

Theorem 2 (Uniform validity of the cross-fitted score test).

Assume A1–A7 in the i.i.d. case or C1–C8 in the clustered case, together with K1 and K3 in Supplementary . Let N=nN=n in the i.i.d. case and N=GN=G in the clustered case, with all score and Jacobian contributions aggregated at the corresponding sampling-unit level. For fixed dzd_{z} and any fixed α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1),

supP∈𝒫N|P{KN(τ0)>χ1,1−α2}−α|⟶0,\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{N}}\left|P\!\left\{\mathrm{K}_{N}(\tau_{0})>\chi^{2}_{1,1-\alpha}\right\}-\alpha\right|\longrightarrow 0,

where 𝒫N=𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{N}=\mathcal{P}_{n} or 𝒫G\mathcal{P}_{G} according to the sampling scheme.

Inverting the score test gives the confidence set

𝒞K,N​(1−α)={t∈ℝ:KN​(t)≤χ1,1−α2},\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{K},N}(1-\alpha)=\{t\in\mathbb{R}:\mathrm{K}_{N}(t)\leq\chi^{2}_{1,1-\alpha}\},

with uniform asymptotic coverage under the same conditions. The proof is in Supplementary . When dz=1d_{z}=1, KN​(t)=ARN​(t)\mathrm{K}_{N}(t)=\mathrm{AR}_{N}(t), using the continuous extension if the adjusted Jacobian vanishes. For multiple instruments, the theorem establishes validity but does not assert a uniform power advantage over AR.

3.3 Survey weights and generated instruments

Survey weights change both the score and, in general, the nuisance targets. Weighting an existing unweighted score need not preserve its centering and orthogonality; the conditional means and exclusion restriction must correspond to the weighted target law. For known weights satisfying 0<cω≤ωi≤Cω<∞0<c_{\omega}\leq\omega_{i}\leq C_{\omega}<\infty, let PωP_{\omega} satisfy d​Pω/d​P=ω/𝔼P​[ω]dP_{\omega}/dP=\omega/\mathbb{E}_{P}[\omega]. If ω\omega is a function of WW alone, the weighted and unweighted conditional means coincide. Otherwise, nuisance fitting and selection use the weighted prediction criterion.

Estimate the conditional means under PωP_{\omega} and form the corresponding cross-fitted residuals. Replace the score and Jacobian contributions by

ψ^iω​(t)=ωi​Z~^iω​(Y~^iω−t​D~^iω),q^iω=−ωi​Z~^iω​D~^iω.\hat{\psi}_{i}^{\omega}(t)=\omega_{i}\hat{\tilde{Z}}_{i}^{\omega}\bigl(\hat{\tilde{Y}}_{i}^{\omega}-t\hat{\tilde{D}}_{i}^{\omega}\bigr),\qquad\hat{q}_{i}^{\omega}=-\omega_{i}\hat{\tilde{Z}}_{i}^{\omega}\hat{\tilde{D}}_{i}^{\omega}.

The AR and score formulas then apply to these contributions, with weighted contributions summed within clusters when appropriate. Weighted moments also replace the moments in (1) for point estimation.

Proposition  in Supplementary establishes validity under the tested-value exclusion condition W-ID(t)(t), the appropriate nuisance-rate conditions, and the required weighted-score moment and non-degeneracy conditions; score inference also requires K1 and K3 for the weighted contributions. In the clustered case, the moment and covariance conditions are imposed on the weighted cluster-score sums.

When the instrument is itself estimated, construction error enters its residual in addition to the error in its conditional mean. The observed-instrument argument does not control this extra term. Construction must also be nested within the folds to avoid using inference observations to generate their own instruments. For example, a leniency instrument for an inference observation is constructed using treatment data outside that observation’s inference cluster fold, and its subsequent residualization follows the same fold-exclusion rule. This makes the constructed instrument function measurable with respect to the training data. Instrument estimation is then treated as an additional nuisance-estimation step. Proposition  in Supplementary extends Theorem 1 under the generated instrument’s exclusion condition, a construction-error rate, and an augmented product-rate condition. These rates control the additional score remainder. Through its identity with AR, score inference is also covered when dz=1d_{z}=1.

4 Monte Carlo Studies

The experiments assess the coverage and informativeness of identification-robust confidence sets and the role of nuisance specification in residualized strength. Supplementary experiments on identification-aware learner selection and selection–inference overlap are reported in Supplementary Table  and Supplementary .

4.1 Simulation design

The core design is a partially linear IV model with correlated Gaussian controls, W∼N⁡(0,ΣW)W\sim N(0,\Sigma_{W}), where (ΣW)i​k=0.5|i−k|(\Sigma_{W})_{ik}=0.5^{|i-k|}, and

Zj\displaystyle Z_{j} =ρ​bj​(W)+1−ρ​eZ,j,\displaystyle=\sqrt{\rho}\,b_{j}(W)+\sqrt{1-\rho}\,e_{Z,j},
D\displaystyle D =W′​βr+fs​∑j=1dzZj+κ​A+ν,\displaystyle=W^{\prime}\beta_{r}+f_{s}\sum_{j=1}^{d_{z}}Z_{j}+\kappa A+\nu,
Y\displaystyle Y =τ0​D+W′​βg+κ​A+ζ.\displaystyle=\tau_{0}D+W^{\prime}\beta_{g}+\kappa A+\zeta.

The innovations eZ,je_{Z,j}, AA, ν\nu, and ζ\zeta are mutually independent standard normals, independent of WW. The shared confounder AA, with κ=0.8\kappa=0.8, creates endogeneity, while τ0=1\tau_{0}=1 is fixed. The functions bjb_{j} are zero, linear, or nonlinear, with fixed population standardization. Thus π0,j=ρ​bj\pi_{0,j}=\sqrt{\rho}\,b_{j} and the treatment conditional mean is r0​(W)=W′​βr+fs​∑jπ0,j​(W)r_{0}(W)=W^{\prime}\beta_{r}+f_{s}\sum_{j}\pi_{0,j}(W).

The core sweeps vary fsf_{s} and, where specified, ρ\rho to span effective-FF values from about 11 to 500500 at a fixed target. Estimated nuisances use five cross-fitting folds. Additional arms examine nonlinear structural functions, clustering, survey weighting, generated instruments with nested selection, and over-identification up to dz=30d_{z}=30. The weighted arm targets τw=1.2\tau_{w}=1.2, distinct from the unweighted target 1.51.5; clustered arms use cluster-aware folds and variances. Supplementary gives the designs, sample sizes, replication counts, and seeds; result tables report Monte Carlo standard errors.

4.2 Cross-fitted AR coverage and power

Figure 1 compares cross-fitted Anderson–Rubin (AR), Wald, and score coverage across oracle, estimated-linear, nonlinear, and over-identified settings, each with at least 1,0001,000 replications. Across these and the additional nonlinear-nuisance settings in Supplementary Table , AR coverage ranges from 0.9380.938 to 0.9680.968, against nominal 0.950.95. At the two calibrated flexible-nuisance points, with median effective-FF of 8.48.4 and 29.129.1, coverage is 0.9510.951 and 0.9490.949; Wald coverage is 0.9670.967 and 0.9590.959. Under weak just-identification, high Wald coverage can reflect unstable estimates and inflated standard errors. Under over-identification, Wald instead undercovers, reaching 0.910.91 at dz=5d_{z}=5 and 0.800.80 at dz=10d_{z}=10 (Supplementary Tables and ).

Dependence and weighting matter for the comparison. Cluster-robust AR covers at 0.9480.948 and 0.9510.951, versus 0.510.51 and 0.690.69 when clustering is ignored. Weighted AR covers τw\tau_{w} at 0.9460.946 and 0.9470.947; unweighted inference, centered on a different target, covers it at only 0.590.59 and 0.090.09 (Supplementary Table ).

The stress experiments reveal finite-sample coverage shortfalls. Across eleven adversarial points, AR coverage ranges from 0.9200.920 to 0.9610.961. The minimum occurs with flexible instrument residualization at effective-F≈33.5F\approx 33.5 (Supplementary Table ). In the combined clustered, generated-instrument, and nested-selection arm, the weak constructed-instrument row covers at 0.9120.912. Its observed-instrument control covers at 0.9560.956 at the same design strength, but construction lowers median effective-FF from 9.69.6 to 2.02.0; a control matched on attained strength covers at 0.9360.936. At moderate strength, constructed and observed instruments cover at 0.9440.944 and 0.9520.952; increasing construction support from m=6m=6 to m=20m=20 cases per cluster leaves constructed coverage at 0.9440.944 (Supplementary Table ).

Supplementary Table  confirms that test-based and extracted-set coverage agree in every reported setting. In the single-instrument sweeps, stronger identification yields narrower finite-length sets and higher rejection rates at τ0+0.5\tau_{0}+0.5. In the structure-matched Angrist–Krueger arm with 5151 clusters, however, AR sets are almost always the whole line at dz=30d_{z}=30: conservative coverage comes with little informativeness (Supplementary Table ).

4.3 Nuisance specification and residualized strength

A separate experiment examines how nuisance specification affects the relationship between instrument prediction and residualized strength. With nonlinear π0\pi_{0}, n=1,500n=1{,}500, and 100100 replications, the random forest predicts ZZ better out of fold than a linear learner (R2=0.50R^{2}=0.50 versus 0.180.18) and leaves less residualized variance (ratios 0.500.50 versus 0.820.82). The strength ranking nevertheless depends on the treatment nuisance (Figure 2). Under correct oracle outcome and treatment nuisances, the forest attains effective-FF about 5757, versus 3434 for ridge residualization, consistent with Proposition 3’s population benchmark. With cross-fitted linear outcome and treatment nuisances, that ordering reverses: about 9393 versus 152152.

The true treatment conditional mean contains the nonlinear component fs​π0​(W)f_{s}\pi_{0}(W). A linear r^\hat{r} does not fully remove this component, leaving structure in the treatment residual that is correlated with predictable instrument variation. A flexible π^\hat{\pi} removes more of this predictable variation from the instrument, leading to a decline in effective-FF in this design. Thus, when random-forest instrument residualization yields a lower effective-FF, the treatment nuisance specification should be checked first.

5 Applications

5.1 Empirical design and diagnostic protocol

Five applications examine the sources of residualized-strength changes and their consequences for effect inference. Figure 3 summarizes the common protocol. We fit outcome, treatment, and instrument nuisances separately using out-of-fold predictions and folds that respect dependence. Instrument fit, calibration, the overfit gap Δπ\Delta_{\pi}, and the residualized variance ratio VπV_{\pi} are read jointly with the first-stage slope and strength. The AR set remains primary at every strength level; learner and split comparisons assess sensitivity. Table 1 reports estimates and inference; Table 2 states each application’s target, assumptions, and theoretical support. Descriptive statistics and diagnostics are in Supplementary Tables – and . Set extraction, including unbounded or empty sets and numerical truncation, follows Supplementary .

Strength is the robust residualized first-stage Wald statistic divided by the numerical rank of the residualized instrument covariance. It equals the Montiel Olea and Pflueger (2013) effective FF for dz=1d_{z}=1. With multiple instruments, it serves only as a strength diagnostic. Over-identified models add score sets under Section 3.2’s conditions, JCUEJ_{\mathrm{CUE}}, and supplementary conditional QLR.

5.2 Comparative evidence across applications

OHIE and baseline Card show learner stability at different strength levels. In OHIE (Finkelstein et al., 2012), lottery selection instruments Medicaid enrollment for twelve-month primary-care visits. Across learners, effective-FF stays around 20002000–21002100, Roof,π2≈0R^{2}_{\mathrm{oof},\pi}\approx 0, and Vπ≈1V_{\pi}\approx 1. Estimates remain near 1.041.04 additional visits, with AR sets close to [0.70,1.39][0.70,1.39]. Card (1995) instruments schooling with college proximity in a log-wage equation. On 3,0103{,}010 men, estimates range from 0.1180.118 to 0.1520.152, effective-FF from 15.215.2 to 18.218.2, and bounded AR sets overlap.

OHIE targets the PLIV coefficient under the survey-weighted law of 23,44123{,}441 complete-case responders. Weights enter the entire pipeline, with household-clustered inference under Proposition ’s regime (b) and weighted-null conditions. The diagnostics support approximately constant instrument propensity among responders; lottery randomization alone fixes it within household-size strata in the lottery population. Response selection still matters: scaling the Lee ITT bounds by the untrimmed first stage gives sensitivity ranges [0.77,2.05][0.77,2.05] with survey weights and [−4.0,4.3][-4.0,4.3] without them (Supplementary Table ).

Examiner leniency instead exposes inference sensitivity despite similar point estimates. Miami–Dade pretrial data (Chyn et al., 2025) use judge leniency to instrument release in a conviction equation. The 91,28291{,}282-case sample retains judges with at least 200200 cases. The leave-one-shift-out instrument is nested within training folds, with court-by-date shift clustering. The examiner random forest fits poorly out of fold despite substantial in-sample fit: Roof,π2<0R^{2}_{\mathrm{oof},\pi}<0, Vπ=1.26V_{\pi}=1.26, and effective-FF falls from ridge’s 20.120.1 to 14.214.2, consistent with overfit dilution. The estimate shifts from −0.480-0.480 to −0.439-0.439, but the AR set widens from [−1.02,−0.04][-1.02,-0.04] to [−1.12,0.10][-1.12,0.10]. With all three nuisances fixed to ridge, the AR set includes zero in two of six sample partitions (Supplementary Table ). Thus the negative estimates suggest that release lowers conviction under the maintained assumptions, while exclusion of zero depends on the learner and split.

Within Card, conditioning changes strength even when instrument fit is stable. Holding college proximity and the 2,1822{,}182-man sample fixed, a five-rung control ladder lowers effective-FF from about 7.57.5 to 2.52.5, non-monotonically. Instrument fit and residualized variance barely change, but the first-stage slope falls from 0.260.26 to 0.120.12: the loss concerns treatment–instrument covariance. Linear-π\pi estimates stay around 0.040.04–0.080.08 (Supplementary ), while AR sets become the whole line at the three richest rungs (Supplementary Table ). The ladder diagnoses concentration, not competing causal specifications: upper rungs include contemporaneous controls, and replacing experience with age moves the canonical estimate’s AR set across zero (Supplementary Table ).

CollegeDistance illustrates a protocol-driven change in diagnosis. Shuffled folds give Roof,π2=0.78R^{2}_{\mathrm{oof},\pi}=0.78; respecting the 4343-group state proxy lowers it to −0.07-0.07, revealing geographic leakage. Flexible-learner estimates remain near zero with AR sets spanning both signs. Separate nuisance selection removes the disagreement produced by coupled learners. With cross-fitting folds defined by the state proxy, all outcome learners have negative out-of-fold R2R^{2} (Supplementary ).

Angrist–Krueger extends the inference comparison to multiple instruments. Three quarter-of-birth instruments give a schooling coefficient near 0.1080.108, with bounded, similar AR, score, and conditional-QLR sets (Supplementary Table ). With thirty quarter-of-birth-by-year interactions, two-stage least squares moves toward OLS with apparent Wald precision, while identification-robust sets are uninformative. At 5151 state-of-birth clusters, the thirty-instrument critical value approaches the clustered AR tail statistic’s cluster-count ceiling (Supplementary ). Full application details are in Supplementary –.

5.3 Cross-application synthesis

The applications show why point-estimate stability and first-stage fit cannot substitute for effect inference. A stable estimate may accompany a wide or unbounded AR set, and a strength change must be traced through folds and nuisance specification before being attributed to instrument learning. Diagnostics identify plausible sources of sensitivity; AR sets describe compatible effect values under the maintained model and IV assumptions.

Figure 4 summarizes learner sensitivity and the fixed-sample control ladder. Differences across populations and designs prevent cross-application strength levels from isolating a common mechanism. Section 4.3 supplies the complementary comparison under known truth, tracing the nuisance-specification reversal through the treatment residual.

6 Discussion and Conclusion

The population result and the empirical diagnostics answer different questions. Proposition 3 ranks instrument residualizations for a fixed conditioning set and a correctly specified treatment nuisance. The applications assess why realized estimates and confidence sets vary when learners, folds, or controls change. Their diagnostic patterns support specific interpretations, but do not uniquely identify a source of weakness or validate the IV assumptions.

The concentration result is related to classical optimal-instruments theory (Amemiya, 1974; Chamberlain, 1987; Newey, 1990), which chooses an instrument transformation h⁡(Z,W)h(Z,W) to attain an efficiency bound under strong identification. Here the instrument is fixed and the choice is its residualization π\pi. Within this class, the two criteria coincide under conditional homoskedasticity of the score, where Var⁡(τ^)∝1/(n​C)\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau})\propto 1/(nC) is exact (Supplementary ). Under bounded conditional heteroskedasticity, CC ranks identification strength up to constants rather than exactly tracking the sandwich variance.

The scope of inference is limited by both the target model and the sampling assumptions. We maintain a homogeneous-coefficient PLIV approximation; under heterogeneity, the causal interpretation depends on the treatment and instrument, as Table 2 records. The clustered validity results are asymptotic in the number of independent clusters and require nuisance-rate conditions. They do not guarantee finite-sample coverage for sparse generated instruments or many instruments with few clusters. Section 4 documents coverage shortfalls as well as near-nominal performance. Moreover, coverage at the true parameter does not make an unbounded set informative.

Two extensions remain useful. The cross-fitted AR moment contains a second-order product of nuisance errors scaled by the tested effect, so rate conditions can become more demanding at distant candidate values. A locally robust corrected moment (Chernozhukov et al., 2022) could address these terms directly. The identification-aware selector also warrants further study: its validity conditions and its finite-sample accuracy are distinct, and the present paired experiments do not establish an accuracy gain.

Flexible instrument residualization has no inherent population concentration cost under the maintained model and a correctly specified treatment nuisance. In empirical work, this benchmark supports joint reporting of nuisance diagnostics, residualized strength, and identification-robust confidence sets, with the estimand and IV assumptions stated explicitly.
